messages.content:
Alex Chen
DATA 4000
27 December 2023
ShotQuality: A Look Into Modern Basketball Analytics
I. Introduction
Within any sport, the objective is to finish atop the rest of the competition. In order to achieve this, players and teams will use all possible information they deem valuable in order to improve or gain a competitive advantage. Within the past decade, an analytics-based approach to the game of basketball has taken the NBA by storm, most notably leading to a drastic increase of 3-pointers being attempted by every team, which is shown in Item 1 of the appendix. With its point value being 1.5 times greater than a 2-point shot, even less efficient marks from 3 could result in more overall points scored. Also, by analyzing the overall efficiency of different shot types, the most efficient shots in basketball were deemed to be 3-pointers and shots directly around the rim (layups and dunks), which can be seen from Item 2 in the appendix. Since then, there have been constant debates over the utility of analytics versus a more traditional approach. However, analytics in the modern NBA is not just about taking more 3-pointers and layups because they are more efficient. With much larger access to data than ever before, coaches, players, and even fans have access to a very powerful tool that gives much more context beyond simply how efficient a certain shot type is. ShotQuality is an expected value that involves the point value of a given shot and the likelihood of said shot going in, with over 90 variables going into calculating this likelihood. An algorithm decides which of these variables are most important for a given shot. Variables such as who is taking the shot, how good they are at that type of shot, who is defending them, how far away the defender is, and many more are considered when creating an accurate estimate of the likelihood of a shot going in. As stated before, this one statistic pulls in a vast amount of information and context to come to a conclusion on exactly how good a shot is.  
	While focusing on ShotQuality through the lens of the NBA, I want to analyze what it can tell a team, player, or a coach about how to be successful in the modern game, whether that be analyzing ShotQuality statistics of an individual player to seek improvement, or looking to acquire players who fit the style of a team. Much of this has been done at the college level, as over 60 teams used its services the previous season, including Men’s National Champion UConn. With its success in College Basketball, it can be explored how its analysis will translate to the NBA. Second, I will include ShotQuality statistics into analysis of trends of successful teams and players in recent years. I intend on starting with analyzing ShotQuality by the difference in positions in the modern NBA. More specifically, I want to place an emphasis on the center (also referred to as “big man/big”) position through the lens of ShotQuality. Throughout the recent years of the NBA, successful teams have been led by perimeter players (guards and forwards). However, within the past few years, we have seen two teams led by big men win championships. Even in terms of individual success, a big has won the MVP in the previous five seasons, and in the past two, the top three players in MVP voting have all been the same big men: Nikola Jokic, Joel Embiid, and Giannis Antetokoumpo. Over the recent years, these three players have consistently led their teams to the top of the standings. I hypothesize that the role of a center/big has changed, and this has contributed to the rise in successful bigs in the modern NBA. I plan to explore this hypothesis through the lens of ShotQuality hand in hand with other counting and advanced statistics to discover if this trend can be explained, what is different about the current big man position from the position 5-10 years ago, and if this trend is here to stay.
II. Data
	On ShotQuality’s website, there is some NBA data that can be accessed freely, where we are able to look at player and team statistics over each season from the past 4 NBA seasons (2020-23). However, some of the more in-depth data that it produces is behind a paywall. For now, there are enough variables from the free dataset to look at. Variables of interest from the player data include SQ PPP (ShotQuality Points Per Possession), Rim and 3 Rate, as well as Good and Bad Possession Rates. From the team standings dataset, I will inspect adjusted Offensive and Defensive ShotQuality, team Rim and 3 Rate, as well as Record Luck. 
To make up for the data that I do not have access to, in R, the packages `nbastatR` and `hoopR` have a plethora of NBA data to join hand in hand with ShotQuality. The `nbastatR` package takes data from Basketball Reference, which has a wide variety of both counting statistics and advanced statistics for players and teams, in which we can perform analyses including ShotQuality variables of interest. This dataset also contains players’ listed position groups: Guard, Forward, and Center. The `hoopR` package gives access to play-by-play data, giving information about the results of each play, including the shot’s coordinates, the type of play, a brief summary of what happened, as well as the players and teams involved. It also contains logical variables that will allow for us to easily filter only shooting or scoring plays. While we do not have access to all of the data provided by ShotQuality, I hope to use the play-by-play data to make visualizations like shot charts. With all three of these datasets, I have access to the last four NBA seasons to perform analyses. Variables from these dataset and their definitions can be found under this section of the appendix. 

III. Shortcomings of ShotQuality / Addition of CleaningTheGlass
	Although the ShotQuality website provides very informative summary statistics, as mentioned before, the more specific data lies behind a paywall, which is $500 for the entire NBA. This includes the SQ Passing Points Generated variable. I will use the summary statistics in my analysis of positions, and will be able to use them to analyze trends between successful teams. But for more in-depth analyses, I will not have access to specific games, or be able to differentiate between regular season and playoffs. Additionally, for analysis of trends, since the data only goes back four years, I do not think it will provide important evidence of the change in the role of the center position. For trends and more in-depth analyses, I will use the nbastatR package as well as the CleaningTheGlass website, which also requires a subscription of $5 a month, but is much more affordable for the scope of this project. It contains advanced statistics for players and teams, as well as shooting frequency and accuracy summaries, and allows me to differentiate from regular season and the playoffs. It also provides me with new position groups, which I believe better describe a player’s role on their team. These positions and how they are defined can be found in Item 1.a of this section. Below that are any variables of interest and their definitions. 
IV. Data Cleaning
	For both of my upcoming player models, I will be joining the ShotQuality, nbastatR, and CleaningTheGlass datasets together by player over the 2023 season, and then by the past four seasons (2020-23). This posed multiple problems with data cleanliness. First, by using the full_join() function in R (Item 1.a) , not only were there many missing values within each respective dataset, but there were also multiple entries for the same player. To make sure that I had only one entry per player, I used the distinct() function (Item 1.b). Next, through investigating each of the datasets, I realized that not every player is in all three datasets. It is then when I switched to an inner_join(), which vastly reduced the number of missing values within each variable (Item 1.c). Lastly, when expanding over to the full dataset, I noticed that some of the columns in the CleaningTheGlass dataset had different names depending on the year, which was a problem as one of those variables was significant in a 2023 season model. To resolve this problem, I created a new variable that encompassed all four seasons using the case_when() function (Item 1.d). 
V. Center/Big Trend Analysis: Exploration
	In the introduction, I hypothesized that the role of the center position has changed in recent years. One of the ways that it has changed is that centers are being asked to attempt way more three-pointers than ever before. Item 1 is a visualization that shows the distribution of total three pointers attempted by position (Guard, Forward, Center). Starting in the 2001-02 season, it is clear that not many centers are even attempting three-pointers, and much less compared to guards and forwards. As we discussed in the introduction, three-point attempts have gone up each year, especially from 2012 (Introduction Item 2). Following this idea, starting from around the 2015-16 season, we notice the third and fourth quartiles of the distribution for centers start to increase dramatically. Although centers still attempt less three-pointers overall compared to the rest of the NBA, it is clear that centers are being asked to shoot many more three-pointers than they were even 7 years ago. 
	Additionally, using the CleaningTheGlass position groups, I conducted One-Way ANOVA analyses to see if there were significant differences by position groups in ShotQuality Statistics during the 2022-23 season. First, I conducted an analysis on ShotQuality Points Per Possession by position. Item 2 shows a density plot of each position’s distribution of ShotQuality Points Per Possession. The distribution of Bigs is centered slightly towards the right of the others, and it also has a heavier right tail. Item 3 shows the counts and group means and counts for each position group, where the mean for Bigs stands out. Section a of Item 3 shows the ANOVA results for ShotQuality Points Per Possession by position, yielding a highly significant p-value (p < 2e-16). Looking at the density plot and the group means, it is likely that this significant difference comes from the big position. I also conducted a One-Way ANOVA of the remaining ShotQuality Player variables, which all yielded very significant p-values, showing there is a difference in each statistic by position. These results can be found in item 4 in this section of the appendix. From these results, we can see that there is a significant difference in ShotQuality statistics by position, and through visualizing it, we see that Bigs average a significantly higher SQ PPP than other positions. 
VI. ShotQuality Points Per Possession Exploration
	In order to better understand a player’s SQ PPP, I have run two exploratory models, one including other ShotQuality statistics, and one without. These models are run first on just the 2022-23 season, as there were structural issues with the data for all four years. For example, when joining the respective data, players’ data would replicate to create a sample size 4 times larger than expected. Even in the 2023 dataset, some players would replicate if they had played for multiple teams within that season. After cleaning the 2023 data to get distinct entries, I was able to produce a sample of 555 players. After removing entries with missing values, the models ran using a sample of 410 players. Once the structural issues were fixed, I was able to expand the model onto the full sample size from the past four seasons. Both models were run on numeric variables from ShotQuality, nbastatR, and CleaningTheGlass. 
	The first stepwise linear regression model tries to predict Shot Quality Points Per Possession with the variables listed in Item 1.a in the appendix. Using backward selection, I landed on a model using 11 variables, each of them significant at the .05 level. The second stepwise linear regression model is a repetition of the first (Item 1.b), except for the removal of the ShotQuality statistics: Possessions, Good Possession Rate, and Bad Possession Rate. Using backward selection, I landed on a model using 8 variables, with 6 of them being significant on the .05 level. The variables used, the Residual Plot and Normal Quantile Plot for both models are listed in their respective sections. For each model, the nonconstant variance assumption holds, and outside of a little deviation at the tails, the Normal Quantile Plots suggest no break in the normality assumption, and the samples are large enough. The p-values for the variables in both models can be found in this section of the appendix below the respective plots.
VII. Model Building/Choices
	In both of my exploratory models, using backward selection posed problems with multicollinearity, as some variables correlated very strongly with each other. For example, Effective Field Goal Percentage and True Shooting Percentage both appeared in the exploratory SQ PPP model, which are similar measurements of shooting accuracy. Thus, for variables like this, it is not necessary to include both in a model. Additionally, to deal with multicollinearity, I switched from a backward selection process to an automated forward selection process. Originally, in the exploratory models, because of the lack of cleanliness in the data, I was unable to run a forward selection model due to the missing values. Along with this, I paid more attention to the VIF scores for each variable within the models, examining anything with a VIF above 5. If a variable had a VIF of above 5, I went back to observe which variable it highly correlated with, and made a decision on whether or not to keep it in the model. For example, by looking at the correlation matrix presented in Item 1 of this section, we see that there was a strong relationship between OWS (Offensive Win Shares) and VORP (Value Over Replacement Player). Interestingly, we see that True Shooting Percentage, Good Possession Rate, and Bad Possession rate, are all related (which makes sense), but do not have alarmingly high VIF scores in the model. If one of these variables had a high VIF and was not significant to the model, I decided to remove it from the model or from the selection process entirely. 
VIII. Center/Big Trend Analysis: Final Model
	Through forward selection, the final model for the 2023 season in predicting if a player plays the Big position or not has 7 variables listed in Item 1.b of this section. 6 of these variables ended up with significant p-values. Three Point Rate was not statistically significant, which makes sense, as we have explored how centers are attempting more three pointers than they used to. The variables with the highest significance were Assist Percentage, Turnover Percentage, and PER. Usage Rate was also significant with a very high estimate. Variables that increased the odds that a player was a Big were PER (Player Efficiency Rating) and Turnover Percentage. Variables that decreased the odds were Assist Percentage and Usage Rate. Assists and Usage go hand in hand: it makes intuitive sense that Bigs would assist on a lower percentage of their teammates shots while being used on a smaller percentage of plays. Usually, perimeter players (Points, Combos, and Wings) assist on a majority of the team’s shots. Additionally, the odds that a player was a Big increased as Turnover Percentage increased. This can also explain why, although Bigs assist their teammates at a lower rate than other positions, they also turn the ball over at a higher rate. Generally, Bigs are seen as less skilled with the ball, so it would make sense that they turn the ball over at a higher rate than other positions. Through our One-Way ANOVA analyses of ShotQuality statistics, I am not surprised to see that PER increased the odds. The model for the 2023 season predicted the correct position with 87.8% accuracy. I ran the same exact model on the 2022, 2021, and 2020 NBA seasons to explore how the model performed in prediction accuracy. In each of these seasons, the model predicted the accurate position 87.1%, 88.6%, and 85.7%, for those respective seasons (Item 1.e). Also, the McFadden’s R Squared values for each year fall in the desired interval of 0.2 to 0.6, showing that the model is a good fit and not artificially inflated (Item 1.f). The estimates, p-values, change in odds, and VIF scores of the model can be found in this section of the appendix (Item 1.d). Although some players like Nikola Jokic, Joel Embiid, and Giannis Antetokounmpo are paving the way for a new style of Bigs, the position as a whole is still less “skilled” than the others. 
IX. ShotQuality Points Per Possession Final Model
	For my Final ShotQuality Points Per Possession Model, I decided to include the ShotQuality statistics. Using the 2023 season, the forward selection process yielded a model with 11 variables which are listed below in the appendix. Nine of these variables were significant, with an additional variable that was borderline insignificant (Possessions). Additionally, the VIF scores for OWS and VORP were both above 5, but I decided to leave them in the model, as they were both significant. Removing either of them from the model lowered the R-Squared value. For the 2023 model, the R-Squared value came out to 0.927, meaning 92.7% of variability of SQ PPP can be explained by the model. The variables with the strongest positive relationships were True Shooting Percentage, Good Possession Rate, and Free Throw Rate. For True Shooting Percentage, this displays how the accuracy of the player taking the shot is taken into account when calculating a ShotQuality score. This also makes sense for Good Possession Rate, as if a player has more good possessions, their ShotQuality Points Per Possession is expected to be higher. The reverse is true for Bad Possession Rate, which is displayed in the model. Lastly, going into this project, Free Throw Rate was not something that I expected to be this influential. If a player shoots free throws accurately, it should be a goal for that player to increase the amount of times they go to the free throw line. To see how this model performed, I ran the same exact formula using a dataset of each player from the past four years (a sample of over 1600). With the increased sample size, all 11 variables in the model were significant. The same main variables that were very significant in the 2023 model remained that way. Variables like Possessions and Three Point Rate that were not significant in the 2023 model were highly significant (p = 6.70e-07, p = 2.31e-05). Interestingly, the R-Squared value dipped to 0.828, meaning only 82.8% of the variability in SQ PPP can be explained by our full model. The full results of the model can be found under this section of the appendix (Items 1.e and 1.f). 
	To explore the four most significant variables further, I reduced the model to include just True Shooting Percentage, Good Possession Rate, Bad Possession Rate, and Free Throw Rate. The results for the 2023 model and the full model can be found in items 1.g and 1.h. In both models, all four variables were very significant (p <2e-16), while all variables had a VIF score below three. In the 2023 model, the R-squared value was 0.921. Compared to the R-squared value of 0.927 in the final model, there is almost no difference in performance between the two models, which demonstrates how influential these four variables are in determining a player’s ShotQuality Points Per Possession. However, this did not solve the problem of the full model performing worse, as the R-squared value for the model covering all four seasons was 0.813. Again, there is not a noticeable dropoff in performance from the final model and the reduced model, but despite the larger sample size, a discussion must be had as to why this model performed worse. I believe one potential problem arises with the assumption of independent observations. Is each player’s performance independent on how they performed in the prior season? Although there is no way to truly measure this, one would have to imagine that some dependence exists from season to season if the same player exists multiple times in the dataset. I will discuss a way to combat this in the Extensions / Limitations section.
X. Trend Analysis: NBA Teams’ ShotQuality and CleaningTheGlass Ranks
	With data from the previous four NBA seasons, we will look to find any commonalities in ShotQuality and CleaningTheGlass statistics between teams that have made the NBA Finals. In order to do this, I will observe where each team ranked relative to the season that they played in. One limitation of the free ShotQuality rankings is that it spans throughout the regular and postseason, and there is no way to extract just the regular season. To get some sort of comparison of ShotQuality and CleaningTheGlass, I took similar statistics from CleaningTheGlass’ team summary data, and observed where the same finals teams ranked. Some explanation of the differences between the two rankings can be attributed to the time periods that they cover. ShotQuality covers the regular season and the playoffs, while these CleaningTheGlass Rankings cover just the regular season.  
	Item 1 shows the rankings of each of the past 8 finals teams in ShotQuality summary statistics. Six out of the 8 teams ranked in the top 10 for Adjusted ShotQuality. The two teams that did not were both the Miami Heat, once in 2020 and again in 2023. Additionally, all 8 teams ranked in the top 10 in either offensive or defensive ShotQuality. Teams like Denver, Boston, and Golden State that fell outside the top 10 on one side of the ball, but made up for it by ranking very high on the other. Interestingly, only two teams ranked in the top 10 of Rim and 3 rate, with half these teams ranked in the bottom half of the NBA. Additionally, only one team ranked in the top 10 of record luck. Note that the Miami Heat, being the only two teams outside the top 10 in Adjusted ShotQuality, made it to the finals in two different ways, being stronger on the offensive end in 2020 and stronger on the defensive end in 2023. 
	In addition to looking at the trends of finals teams from the past four years, I also looked graphically at the 2023 season to see what these statistics can tell us about a team’s overall win percentage. Item 2.a is a plot of teams’ Adjusted Shot Quality ranking vs. their win percentage ranking. Instead of looking at the actual number, we see how teams are relative to their peers. With this, we see a strong association that if a team ranks high in Adjusted Shot Quality, they also rank towards the top of the league in win percentage. This is also reflected by the fact that all but two of the past 8 teams to make the NBA Finals ranked in the top 10 in this statistic. Item 2.d is a similar plot exploring the relationship of Rim and 3 Rate ranking vs. win percentage ranking. Similar to our exploration of the past 8 finals teams, there does not seem to be an association between how many of a team’s shots come from the rim and 3 and winning. This leads me to believe that this is more of an accuracy issue, or that too many shots from that area would become too predictable. 
	Item 3 shows the rankings of the eight finals teams in Per 100 Possessions statistics provided by CleaningTheGlass, although just looking at the regular season. Similar to Adjusted ShotQuality, 7 of 8 teams ranked inside the top 10 in Point Differential, in fact they all ranked 7th or higher, except for the 2023 Miami Heat, who ranked 20th. Furthermore, the same condition of each team ranking top 10 on either offense or defense still holds. In terms of expected wins, 7 of the 8 teams ranked 7th or higher, except the 2023 Miami Heat, who again ranked 20th. Although CleaningTheGlass only looks at the regular season, it was interesting to see that many of the conditions that held for the teams’ ShotQuality rankings still held for CleaningTheGlass. After analyzing both tables, it seems that one team is a glaring outlier, which I would like to analyze further. 
XI. Team of interest – 2022-23 Miami Heat
	In the 2022-23 NBA playoffs, the Miami Heat entered as the 8th seed in the Eastern Conference and made a run to the NBA Finals, making them the second team in NBA history to do so, and the first team to do so in a full season. In their path to the finals, they defeated the 1st seed Milwaukee Bucks and 2nd seed Boston Celtics, the teams with the best two overall records that season. Through some analysis of ShotQuality trends, and in-depth analysis on CleaningTheGlass, I will try to pinpoint what changed in order for this run to take place. First, I will take a look at overall team differences in shooting accuracy from CleaningTheGlass from the regular season to the playoffs. Focusing on the Heat, I will analyze individual players’ improvements from the regular season to the playoffs. Additionally, I will analyze how Miami fared in certain statistics from the regular season to the playoffs to see if it is possible to pinpoint where these changes occurred. 
XII. 2023 Miami Heat Shooting Accuracy Improvements
	Using the Shooting Accuracy datasets on CleaningTheGlass, we can measure teams’ shooting accuracy improvements from the regular season to the playoffs. As of the 2020-21 NBA season, the NBA has introduced a Play-In Tournament to decide the 7th and 8th seeds for the playoffs. We will only include the teams who made it through the Play-In Tournament to the playoffs, as teams who were eliminated may have only played 1-2 games. Item 1 displays the difference in shooting accuracy at the rim (x) and the difference of three point accuracy (y) from the playoffs to the regular season for the 2022-23 playoff teams. From this visualization, we can see that on average, teams regressed in accuracy in both categories. Looking at the Heat, although they regressed in accuracy at the rim, Miami’s three point accuracy increased by a noticeable amount compared to any other team. Item 2 displays the difference in Miami Heat players’ shooting accuracy on two point shots (x) and the difference of three point accuracy (y) from the playoffs to the regular season in 2023. For players who played enough minutes, most regressed in two point shot accuracy. However, nearly every single player improved their individual three point accuracy, which reflects Item 1. One last thing to note is that Caleb Martin improved both his two point and three point accuracy by a decent margin, while being a starter. His impact on the Heat’s success led him to be just one vote short of winning the Eastern Conference Finals MVP award (Item 3). 
XIII. Caleb Martin and Duncan Robinson
	To explore the second plot from the previous section further, I removed the text aesthetic and replaced it with a size aesthetic which showed how many minutes each player played in the playoffs (Items 1 and 2). Through this, I was able to observe that Caleb Martin and Duncan Robinson improved both their two-point and three-point percentages, while playing enough minutes to make an impact Martin played about 32 minutes a game as a starter, and Robinson played 17 minutes a game off the bench. After observing this, I want to take a deeper look to see if these improvements could have been foreseen, or if they should have been expected. I will conduct this analysis through observing how they each fared in some of the significant variables from the SQ PPP model over the past four years. In addition, I will create shot charts from the 2023 regular season using the play-by-play data available in the hoopR package. Since this dataset does not have access to the playoffs, I will look at shot charts provided by outside sources that do have access to the playoffs, provided by the Positive Residual (Item 3). Lastly, I will look at shooting frequency statistics which can be found on CleaningTheGlass. 
XIV. Could We Have Seen This Coming?
	First, we will look at plots that explore how Martin and Robinson performed on a year-to-year basis leading up to the 2023 playoffs. It is important to note that while Robinson spent all four years of this span with the Heat, Martin played with the Charlotte Hornets in the 2020 and 2021 seasons before signing with Miami. We must also note that Martin only played 18 games in 2020 and Robinson only played 41 games in 2023, thus their percentages might be impacted by the smaller sample size. Looking at Martin’s overall SQ PPP, it has improved on a yearly basis since 2021 (Item 1.a). However, we do not see the same year-to-year improvement with his True Shooting Percentage and Good Possession Rate, which improved from 2021 to 2022, but dipped down in 2023 (Items 1.d and 1.b). Interestingly, while this occurred, his Bad Possession Rate also dropped slightly from 2022 to 2023 (Item 1.c). Robinson definitely has played at this level before, as seen by his percentages in 2020, but over the past few years, we saw how his performance declined in many of these statistics. His SQ PPP has declined each year since 2020, as well as his True Shooting Percentage and Good Possession Rate, while his Bad Possession Rate stayed mostly the same, before increasing slightly in 2023 (Items 1.a-1.d). For Robinson, his 2020 season shows that he is capable of shooting as accurately as he did in the playoffs. However, the decline in performance in the years leading up to the 2023 playoffs would have made it difficult to anticipate his accuracy improving to the degree that it did. 
XV. A Change in Shot Selection
	To explore how their accuracies improved, I created shot charts for each individual player using the play-by-play data provided in the hoopR package. Item 1 displays the shot chart that I created for Caleb Martin. Item 2 displays the shot chart that I created for Duncan Robinson. Robinson’s chart is less dense due to the fact that he played less games in this regular season compared to Martin. This is my first time ever making a shot chart, and I was unsuccessful in getting the actual court to show up, but we can see that the coordinates mimic the halfcourt setting, and we can make an outline of the three point line. In both shot charts, we see much more concentrated areas around the three point line. From the rim, Caleb Martin made 65% of his shots on 158 shot attempts in the regular season, which put him in the 42nd percentile for his position. From the rim, Duncan Robinson made 79% of his shots on just 14 attempts, which put him at the 79th percentile for his position. From three, Caleb Martin shot 37% (56th percentile), and Duncan Robinson shot 33% (28th percentile). These statistics can be found under Item 5 of this section of the appendix. 
	Through looking at their playoff shot charts provided by Positive Residual, we can visualize where their accuracies improved. One thing to note is that this chart is not measuring makes and misses, but an overall True Shooting percentage from that area, relative to the average. A red dot signifies that a player is shooting above average from that area, where a blue dot shows the opposite. Item 3 displays Caleb Martin’s shot chart from the 2023 Playoffs, where we see that he is shooting less overall from midrange and shooting more accurately from that area, while also shooting above average from the rim and from three. Item 4 displays Duncan Robinson’s shot chart from the 2023 Playoffs, where we see that his three point accuracy improved dramatically, shooting above average in almost all areas (his accuracy in the regular season placed him at the 28th percentile for his position). Additionally, he continues to shoot accurately from the rim. However, analyzing overall shot charts from the regular season to the playoffs do not take into account that the playoffs are a smaller sample size, which may influence the total number of attempts in any given area. 
	To bridge that gap, I looked at their differences in total shooting frequency from different areas from the regular season to the playoffs. Item 6 displays a stacked bar plot of Caleb Martin’s shooting frequency from different areas of the court. From the regular season to the playoffs, Martin took 5% less of his shots from the midrange area, which turned into 5% more three point shots. I note this 5% drop in midrange shots because he only made 41% of his shots from that distance (56th percentile). Taking less midrange shots increased his overall accuracy, as it improved to 50% (84th percentile) in the playoffs. Additionally, his rim accuracy improved to 72%, and his three point accuracy improved to 42%. While I believe some improvement in shooting accuracy can simply be explained by shooting better over a certain period of time, especially during a small sample size like the playoffs, it is interesting to note how his change in shot selection affected his accuracy on all three levels of the court. 
Item 7 displays the same plot, but for Duncan Robinson. From the regular season to the playoffs, Robinson doubled the amount of shots that he was taking at the rim, going from 7% (14 total shots) to 15% of his shots. Overall, he shot 18/22 from the rim (82%). Although he still did not attempt many, the playoffs are a much smaller sample size than the regular season, as he attempted more shots from the rim in about half as many games played. I believe this improves not only his performance but the team’s performance. By taking (and making) more shots at the rim, the defense has to respect that ability of his game, which in turn will get him better shots from 3. While it may not be the sole reason, this could explain how his accuracy improved to 41% from three. Shot selection is at the heart of each calculation of ShotQuality, thus it is very important for players and teams to improve, in order to have higher likelihoods of making shots. Whether or not it was intentional, Caleb Martin and Duncan Robinson changed the amount of shots that they were taking in certain areas, which led to improvements in both their overall two-point and three-point accuracy. For the sake of the Miami Heat, their shooting accuracy improvements helped propel one of the most unlikely runs that the NBA has ever seen. 
XVI. Expanding / Limitations
First, I would like to further explore the assumption of independence with the SQ PPP model that I conducted over the past four seasons. Out of curiosity, I looked to see how the 2023 model performs over each of the past three seasons (2022, 2021, and 2020). The year that produced the lowest R-squared value was 2022, with a value of 0.838, which was still higher than that of the full model (Item 2). Through exploration of the full sample from all four years, there are 612 distinct players, in which 169 appear in just one season, 96 appear twice, 121 appear three times, and 226 players have played all four years (Item 1). One way I believe this could be addressed is through a stratified random sampling based on each position group that would have every player appearing in no more than one season. This would yield a sample of 612 where the assumption of independence holds, and my intuition tells me that it would have a higher R-Squared value than my current model.
In terms of my analysis for the Miami Heat, I focused on the offensive side of the ball, looking at shooting accuracies and frequencies. It would be interesting to also look into the defensive side of the ball and see if similar changes existed. Additionally, I would like to have access to play-by-play data for ShotQuality, as I believe a model with the ShotQuality value of each shot as the response variable would be more interesting to look at than that statistic over an entire season. Also, I would like to have access to game logs provided by ShotQuality, as I believe this could provide a much deeper analysis into the 2023 Miami Heat’s historic playoff run. ShotQuality also keeps track of a player’s driving ability, which would have been interesting to look at in the context of Duncan Robinson’s shooting at the rim. Also, I hope to improve my graphical skills, especially in making shot charts so that my graphs more closely resemble those provided by Positive Residual. Lastly, all of the analysis of trends using ShotQuality data only has four full seasons to look at. I am curious to see if the trends that I looked at for finals teams and overall win percentage continue over the next 5-10 years. 
XVII. Conclusion
	Through the lens of ShotQuality and incorporating datasets from nbastatR, hoopR, and CleaningTheGlass, we have attempted to answer some of modern basketball’s biggest questions. We used summary statistics to see what kind of variables go into calculating how good a shot is through my SQ PPP model. Even with the summary statistics, we see how the context of the individual player is taken into account through variables like True Shooting Percentage, and Good and Bad Possession Rates. An additional variable that was surprisingly significant was Free Throw Rate, signifying the importance of the ability to get to the free throw line. Through the use of ANOVA and my logistic regression model, we explored numerically what the role of a Big/Center is in the modern NBA. Through our Logistic Regression Model, we found that, while Bigs are more “efficient,” they assist at a lower rate, turn the ball over at a higher rate, and are used in less plays than other positions. Although there are Bigs like Nikola Jokic, who has the highest Assist Percentage on his team (Item 1.j), the position as a whole is still less skilled in that area. I still am curious to see if the gap in skill lessens as the years go on. At the team level, we took a look at the teams to make the finals within the past 4 years to find any commonalities within their ShotQuality and CleaningTheGlass summary statistics. We also analyzed this graphically, showing a likely association between adjSQ and win percentage. Through our analysis of the past 8 finals teams, we noticed that the 2023 Miami Heat were a glaring outlier that needed to be explored further. Through graphical analysis, we found that, as a team, they greatly improved their shooting accuracy from three. Two players that stood out were Caleb Martin and Duncan Robinson, who’s changes in shot selection contributed to improvements in their two-point and three-point percentages. Their success contributed to their team’s success in making an improbable run to the NBA finals. ShotQuality data is relatively recent, and I anticipate revisiting it in 5-10 years to conduct more analysis when there is even more data to work with.

Based on the provided text, here is a reconstruction of the author's methodological workflow for the ShotQuality Points Per Possession (SQ PPP) model, detailing the failures, underlying issues, pivots, and an evaluation of their proposed solution.

### Methodological Workflow and Pivots for the SQ PPP Model

**1. Initial Plan & First Failure (Data Structure)**

*   **Plan:** The author intended to run two exploratory stepwise linear regression models for the 2022-23 season. The first model would predict SQ PPP using other ShotQuality statistics (Possessions, Good Possession Rate, Bad Possession Rate) along with variables from other datasets. The second model would be the same but exclude these specific ShotQuality statistics.
*   **Failure:** Upon attempting to join the datasets for all four seasons (2020-23), the author discovered severe data replication issues. Players who had played for multiple teams in a single season, or whose data was structured in a way that caused duplication during joins, resulted in a sample size that was artificially inflated (up to 4 times larger than expected).
*   **Underlying Issue:** Poor data integrity and structure in the raw joined datasets, leading to non-distinct observations and violating the assumption of independent data points.

**2. First Pivot (Data Cleaning)**

*   **Action:** To salvage the analysis, the author narrowed the focus to the 2023 season only. They used the `distinct()` function in R to remove duplicate player entries.
*   **Result:** This cleaning process reduced the dataset to 555 players. After removing entries with missing values, the final sample size for the exploratory models was 410 players.

**3. Second Failure (Modeling Method & Multicollinearity)**

*   **Plan:** Using the cleaned 2023 data, the author proceeded with the planned stepwise linear regression models, using backward selection.
*   **Failure:** The backward selection process led to models with significant multicollinearity. The author explicitly states this, giving the example of including both Effective Field Goal Percentage (EFG%) and True Shooting Percentage (TS%), which are highly correlated measures of shooting efficiency. This redundancy can destabilize coefficient estimates and inflate standard errors.
*   **Underlying Issue:** The automated backward selection algorithm included multiple variables that measured similar underlying concepts, a classic case of multicollinearity.

**4. Second Pivot (Model Building Strategy)**

*   **Action:** To address the multicollinearity, the author changed their modeling strategy.
    *   They abandoned backward selection in favor of an **automated forward selection process**.
    *   They began paying closer attention to **VIF (Variance Inflation Factor)** scores for each variable, investigating any with a VIF above 5.
    *   When high VIF variables were identified, they investigated correlations and made deliberate choices about which variable to keep (e.g., keeping a significant variable even with high VIF if its removal degraded model performance, as with OWS and VORP).
*   **Result:** This pivot allowed for a more controlled inclusion of variables and a better-handled model.

**5. Development of the Final 2023 Model**

*   **Action:** Using the new forward selection process on the 2023 data, the author built the final model. They chose to include the ShotQuality statistics.
*   **Result:** The forward selection yielded a model with 11 variables. Nine were significant, and one (Possessions) was borderline. The model had a high R-Squared of 0.927, indicating it explained 92.7% of the variability in SQ PPP. Key predictors included True Shooting Percentage, Good Possession Rate, and Free Throw Rate.

**6. Third Failure (Full Model Performance & Non-Independence)**

*   **Plan:** The author expanded the same model formula to the full dataset of the past four seasons (2020-23), which contained over 1600 player observations.
*   **Failure:** The model's performance degraded, with the R-Squared dropping to 0.828.
*   **Underlying Issue:** The author hypothesized that this was due to a violation of the independence assumption. The dataset contained multiple observations (seasons) for the same players (226 players appeared in all four seasons), meaning a player's performance in one season was likely not independent of their performance in another.

**7. Final Pivot & Proposed Solution (Limitations)**

*   **Action (Analysis):** The author explored a reduced model containing only the four most influential variables (TS%, Good Poss Rate, Bad Poss Rate, FT Rate). This confirmed that these few variables drove most of the predictive power, but it did not fix the R-Squared drop in the full model.
*   **Proposed Solution (in Limitations Section):** To resolve the non-independence issue, the author proposed a **stratified random sampling** method. This would select only one season per player (from the 612 distinct players), ensuring that each observation in the model is independent. They believed this would yield a higher R-Squared.

---

### Evaluation of the Proposed Solution

The question asks whether the proposed solution in the 'Limitations' section would resolve the root cause of the **multicollinearity** issues.

**Conclusion: No, the proposed solution would not resolve the multicollinearity issue.**

*   **Root Cause of Multicollinearity:** The multicollinearity arose because the initial modeling process (backward selection) included multiple highly correlated predictor variables (like EFG% and TS%). This is a problem of variable selection and statistical relationship between predictors.
*   **Author's Actual Fix for Multicollinearity:** The author correctly identified and addressed this by switching to forward selection and actively monitoring VIF scores (Section VII). This is the pivot that resolved the multicollinearity problem.
*   **What the Proposed Solution Addresses:** The proposed stratified random sampling solution is aimed at fixing the **independence of observations** problem (Section XVI). By ensuring each player appears only once in the dataset, it would prevent the violation of the independence assumption that likely caused the drop in R-Squared when the model was expanded to multiple seasons.
*   **Evaluation:** While the proposed solution is a valid and appropriate way to address the non-independence issue, it is unrelated to the multicollinearity issue. The multicollinearity was already mitigated by the change in model-building strategy (forward selection), not by altering the sample. Therefore, the proposed solution would not resolve the root cause of the multicollinearity, as that problem had already been handled separately.
